la:noun:bucca.gloss: the soft part of the cheek puffed or filled out in speaking or eating
senses: the soft part of the cheek puffed or filled out in speaking or eating
one who fills his cheeks in speaking; declaimer, bawler
one who stuffs out his cheeks in eating; parasite
A catchword of uncertain meaning used in a guessing game, possibly equivalent and/or related to English buck buck.
la:noun:bucca.html:
bucca (not buccha), ae, f.
kindred

with βύζω, βυκάνη; Fr. bouche

.
The cheek (puffed or filled out in speaking, eating, etc.; diff. from genae, the side of the face, the cheeks, and from mala, the upper part of the cheek under the eyes; v. sqq.; mostly in plur.; class.): buccam implere, Cato ap. : sufflare buccas,: inflare,: rumpere buccas,to write bombast,: sufflare buccis,.—In violent anger (cf. in Gr. φυσᾶν τὰς γνάθους, δεινὰ φυσᾶν, etc.): quin illis Juppiter ambas Iratus buccas inflet, etc., * : pictus Gallus ... distortus, ejectā linguā, buccis fluentibus,; : fluentes pulsataeque buccae, B. and K.: purpurissatae (rouged), .—In blowing the fire: buccā foculum excitat,—Hence,
Dicere (scribere) quod or quidquid in buccam venit, a colloq. phrase, to speak (write) whatever comes uppermost, ; fin.; 14, 7, 2; .— Also ellipt.: garrimus quidquid in buccam,.—
Meton.
One who fills his cheeks in speaking, a declaimer, bawler: Curtius et Matho buccae, (jactanticuli, qui tantum buccas inflant et nihil dicunt, Schol.); cf.: bucca loquax vetuli cinoedi,: homo durae buccae,; so of a trumpeter: notaeque per oppida buccae,.—
One who stuffs out his cheeks in eating, a parasite, .—
A mouthful: bucca panis,; ; .—
Transf.
From men to animals; of croaking frogs,.—
In gen., a cavity; of the knee-joint, .

la:noun:bucina.html:
būcĭna (not buccĭna), ae, f., = βυκάνη,
a crooked horn or trumpet (while tuba is usually the straight trumpet; cf. Stewech.).
Lit., a shepherd's horn, : bucina inflata,; ; .—
Transf.
A war-trumpet: bello dat signum rauca cruentum Bucina,: quā bucina signum Dira dedit,.—In gen., as a signal employed in changing the four night-watches, and for waking the soldiers (cf. Dict. of Antiq.): te gallorum, illum bucinarum cantus exsuscitat,: ubi secundae vigiliae bucinā datum signum esset,; ; .—
Hence, meton.: ad primam, secundam, etc., bucinam (for vigiliam), at the first, second, etc., watch: ut ad tertiam bucinam praesto essent,.—It was also blown at the end of the evening meal, Nipp. ad loc.—
In other spheres of life; so for calling assemblies of the people: bucina datur: homines ex agris concurrunt,: bucina cogebat priscos ad verba Quirites, .— For designating the hours of the day (which were divided into four parts),; cf. bucino.—
Poet., a kind of circular, winding shell on which Triton blew, Triton's shell, and 337; cf. bucinator.—
Trop.: foedae bucina famae,the trump of ill fame,; cf. bucinator, II.

senses: a papal bull or other official document sealed with a bulla
la:noun:bulla.html:
bulla, ae, f.
root vhal-; Gr. φαλ-; cf. φαλλός, φύλλον
,
any object swelling up, and thus becoming round; hence,
A waterbubble, bubble: ut pluvio perlucida caelo Surgere bulla solet,: crassior,; ; .—Hence,
Trop., a bubble, trifle; vanity: si est homo bulla, eo magis senex,; .—
Any thing rounded by art.
A boss, knob (upon a door, etc.): jussine in splendorem dari bullas has foribus nostris?: bullas aureas ex valvis, auferre, (by such door-studs fortunate or unfortunate days were designated, ).—
A stud in a girdle: notis fulserunt cingula bullis Pallantis pueri,; ; ; .—
The head of a pin in the water-clock, —
Esp., the bulla, a kind of amulet worn upon the neck (mostly of gold), orig. an ornament of the Roman triumphers, in imitation of the Tuscan kings and Lucumones (Plut. Romul. 25; Fest. s. v. sardi, p. 252), but in the more brilliant era of the Romans worn by noble youths, (cf. Ascon. in h. l., acc. to whom bullae of leather were hung upon the necks of the children of freedmen); it was laid aside when they arrived at maturity, and consecrated to the Lares,; cf.: Lares bullati,; acc. to , first hung by Tarquinius Priscus upon the neck of his son; cf. also sqq.; ; ; ; ; .—From the Etruscan custom, called Etruscum aurum, .—Hence the phrase bullā dignus for childish: senior bullā dignissime,.—It was also hung upon the forehead of favorite animals, .

senses: a place for burning funeral pyres (with human remains interred at or near the site)
la:noun:bustum.html:
bustum, i, n.
buro = uro, whence also comburo; cf. burrus, red
, orig.
the place where the bodies of the dead were burned and buried; later also, in gen., for a tomb: bustum proprie dicitur locus, in quo mortuus est combustus et sepultus... ubi vero combustus quis tantummodo, alibi vero est sepultus, is locus ab urendo ustrina vocatur; sed modo busta sepulchra appellamus, Paul. ex Müll.; cf. Serv. ad Verg.

A. 3, 22; 11, 201; .

The place of burning and burying; the funeral-pyre after the burning of the body: semiustaque servant Busta neque avelli possunt, Don. ad loc.; ; ; cf. .—
Transf.
In gen., a mound, tomb (most freq. in the poets): in busto Achilli,: si quis bustum (nam id puto appellari τύμβον) violarit, Solon ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; * ; ; 1, 19, 21; 2 (3), 13, 33; ; ; ; ; —
Trop., of things that, like a tomb, give up a body to destruction; so of the maw of an animal that eats men: viva videns vivo sepeliri viscera busto,seeing the living body enclosed in the living grave,.—So of Tereus, who devoured his son: flet modo, seque vocat bustum miserabile nati,.—Sarcastically, of one who annulled the laws: bustum legum omnium ac religionum,; and: bustum rei publicae,.—Of a battle-field: civilia busta Philippi, Kuin.—
Ad Busta Gallica, a place in Rome, so called from the Gauls who were burned and buried there, Müll.; ; .—
Of a destroyed city, the site, ruins, .—
The burned body itself, the ashes, .

la:verb:bullo.html:
bullo, āre, and bullĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. n.
bulla
,
to be in bubbling motion, to be in a state of ebullition, to bubble.
Form bullo, āre: ubi bullabit vinum, ignem subducito,; ; ; ; ; , 74, § 317.—
Form bullio, īre: bullientes fontes,; ; ; ; .—As v. a. in part. pass.: ammoniacum cum vino et melle mittis in ollam et bullita (sodden, i. e. half-cooked) atteres, dabisque ad bibendum, (1, 45, 5).—
Trop.: indignatione,to boil with rage, fty in a passion,: libidinum incendio bulliebant,.
